artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a permutation $w \in S_n$, let $\mathfrak{S}_w(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ denote its Schubert polynomial, and define
$$\nu_w := \mathfrak{S}_w(1, 1, \dots, 1),$$
the sum of its coefficients. It is known that $\nu_w = 1$ if and only if $w$ is $132$-avoiding (i.e. dominant): there is no triple of indices $i < j < k$ with $a_i < a_k < a_j$, where $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ in one-line notation.

Prove or disprove: $\nu_w = 2$ if and only if the one-line notation $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ contains exactly one occurrence of the pattern $132$, i.e., exactly one triple of indices $i < j < k$ such that $a_i < a_k < a_j$.
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture was proved by Anna Weigandt (2018), who showed that $\nu_w$ equals the number of reduced pipe dreams (or equivalently is bounded below by/related to the number of $132$-patterns), establishing in particular that $\nu_w = 2$ iff $w$ has exactly one $132$-pattern.

status_evidence.title: Schubert polynomials, 132-patterns, and Stanley's conjecture (A. Weigandt)
status_evidence.snippet: Weigandt proves Stanley's conjecture that the number of 132-patterns in w gives a lower bound for the principal specialization of the Schubert polynomial, with equality cases characterizing when $\nu_w = 2$.
status_evidence.claim: Weigandt (2018) proved Stanley's Conjecture 4.1 relating $\nu_w = 2$ to permutations with exactly one 132-pattern.
